title: How to improve your business’s chances of appearing in AI answers
description: A practical guide to website evidence, crawler roles and recorded assistant checks, with the published H4TLT case study and clear limits on result claims.
html:
Updated 16 October 2026. This article replaces earlier claims about a six-week client result, universal AI rankings and scanner capabilities. Those claims should not be used as evidence or as a promise of future results.

A recruitment agency can have a useful website and still be absent when an employer asks ChatGPT for a supplier. That answer deserves investigation. It does not, by itself, tell you whether the problem is the website, the question, the sources selected or the assistant’s particular response.

Start with a question you can test, then keep the evidence attached. A website score, an assistant mentioning your agency and an employer submitting an enquiry are different observations. Putting them in the same green circle saves dashboard space, but makes the business decision rather harder.

Choose the employer question first

Write down what a prospective client might need: a recruitment partner for a particular role, sector or location; evidence that the agency understands the work; or an explanation of how an assignment starts. Use the language that appears in real enquiries where you have permission to use it.

Keep a small, fixed set of questions. Include questions about your named agency and questions that do not mention it. “What does this agency do?” checks a different problem from “Which agency should we consider?” Record the wording before testing, so a disappointing answer does not become a different question.

Make the relevant page useful

Read the page an employer should find. Can they identify the service, the roles covered, the area served, the supplier and the next step? Does the evidence support the claim being made? A list of sectors is less useful than a clear account of the work the agency actually undertakes.

Keep names and relationships consistent across the site. Explain a specialist service’s relationship to its parent company. Publish genuine experience and approved client evidence, with enough context to understand it. A company does not acquire another office because somebody has added a postcode to its structured data.

Check access without treating AI as one visitor

Inspect the HTML returned by the server as well as the finished browser page. If important service information appears only after scripts run, some retrieval tools may miss it. Google Search can process JavaScript, while browser agents may inspect a rendered page. Test the relevant route before prescribing a rebuild.

Crawler controls also have different jobs. OpenAI distinguishes search, potential training and user-requested fetching. Anthropic documents separate crawler roles too. Check the actual user agent, robots rules, response status and any verified firewall evidence. Permission to crawl does not establish that an assistant selected or cited the page.

Use structured data to describe supported facts

Relevant schema can describe the organisation, services, articles and other information visible on a page. Validate the syntax and check the facts. If the page changes, the markup needs checking too.

Google says structured data is not required for its generative search features. It remains useful for eligible rich results, but there is no special schema recipe that guarantees an AI recommendation. Google’s Rich Results Test checks its supported features; an empty result does not establish that a page contains no structured data at all.

An optional llms.txt file can provide a curated map for tools that choose to read it. Keep it accurate if you supply one. It does not replace public content, access controls or the separate work of measuring actual answers.

Record what the assistant actually returned

For each question, save the product, mode, date, relevant location or personalisation settings, answer and cited URLs. Note whether a search visibly ran. Use a fresh context where practical and record any access failure. A consumer product and its provider’s API can produce different observations.

Score the parts separately: whether the agency was mentioned, whether it was described correctly, whether a useful source was cited and whether the answer gave a sensible next step. One favourable screenshot cannot establish a permanent position, and repeating a question until the agency appears makes the record less useful.

Run a separate test with the page supplied explicitly. That can reveal missing or ambiguous information. It does not show that the assistant would have discovered the page unaided.

Repair the fault you can demonstrate

A missing service description needs a content repair. A failed request needs an access investigation. Contradictory company names need reconciliation. Keep the work connected to the finding, then repeat the same check after publication.

Watch search data and consent-based website analytics alongside the answer records. An assistant citation, a referred visit and a qualified enquiry each need their own evidence. Agree a review schedule, rather than promising that every business will appear in answers after a fixed number of weeks.

Where ScopeSite’s work fits

Our published H4TLT case study sets out the approved evidence for work with Hear 4 The Long Term, a workplace hearing-surveillance business. Read its scope directly; it is not a recruitment result or a timetable for another company.

title: Why your business may be missing from an AI answer, and what to check
description: How to check delivered HTML, crawler access, structured data and observed assistant answers without treating a scan as a ranking guarantee.
html:
Updated 16 October 2026. This article replaces unsupported agency allegations, an unverified events-business case story and universal claims about AI crawling and result timelines. The guidance below distinguishes technical findings from observed assistant answers.

An absent recommendation is a starting point for an investigation. It is a poor diagnosis on its own. The assistant may have interpreted the question differently, selected other sources or answered without a fresh search. There may also be a real problem with the website. You need evidence to tell those possibilities apart.

For a recruitment owner, the question is whether an employer can find the relevant service, understand the agency’s experience and start a conversation. Test that before declaring the business invisible.

Capture the answer before changing the site

Save the exact question, the product and mode, the date, any relevant location setting, the answer and its cited URLs. Record whether the session was signed in or carried previous conversation context. If the product was inaccessible or the request failed, record the failure separately from an answer that omitted the business.

Keep a small set of realistic buyer questions fixed for later comparison. Test the named agency as well as an unbranded supplier question. Avoid changing the wording repeatedly until a preferred result appears; the original evidence still needs explaining.

Compare the first response with the finished page

Open the relevant service page and inspect the HTML returned by its URL. Then compare it with the rendered browser page. Look for the important facts: company identity, service scope, roles covered, location and a usable enquiry link.

If those facts appear only after JavaScript runs, a retrieval tool that does not render scripts may miss them. That finding can justify a rendering repair. It does not establish that every AI system sees a blank page. Google Search can render JavaScript, and browser agents may use the rendered screen, page structure and accessibility information.

Check the actual delivery before blaming the platform name. Two sites built with the same framework can expose their content differently. A full rebuild should answer an observed problem that a smaller change cannot reasonably solve.

Check the relevant access controls

Read the robots rules for the actual user agent and URL. Inspect response status codes and any available verified crawler or firewall records. A successful request from your own laptop does not prove what a service’s crawler received.

Separate search crawling, potential model training and user-requested fetching. OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity document distinct roles. Blocking a training crawler does not automatically prove absence from every answer route; allowing one does not guarantee inclusion. Keep private account pages and reports private while investigating public discovery.

Look for an information problem

Ask someone unfamiliar with the agency to identify its specialism, the businesses it serves and how to enquire. If the page requires several guesses, an assistant may also produce an incomplete description. Fix the ambiguous wording because it matters to the buyer.

Check for conflicting company names, expired offers, unsupported testimonials and service claims that differ across pages. Make internal links useful and descriptive. A heading called “Solutions” followed by another heading called “Excellence” can leave everybody fully informed about absolutely nothing.

You can supply the page to an assistant and ask factual questions as a separate extraction test. Label that test clearly. Success with a supplied URL does not demonstrate unaided discovery.

Validate schema without making it a gatekeeper

Structured data should describe supported facts visible on the page. Validate it and inspect the relationships between the organisation, service and article. Do not add reviews, offices or qualifications merely to make the graph look more substantial.

Google’s current guidance says structured data is not a requirement for its generative search features. The Rich Results Test covers supported Google features, while a general schema validator examines the wider vocabulary. Passing either check does not certify that an assistant will cite the business.

Treat llms.txt as an optional maintained resource for tools that choose to use it. It is not an access-control file, and Google Search says it does not use it to improve or reduce search visibility.

Measure performance with its limits attached

Investigate slow or failed responses, broken navigation and poor mobile usability. Record the URL, device conditions, date and test method. A lab performance score and real-user field measurements answer different questions, and some pages have insufficient field data.

There is no verified universal 200-millisecond abandonment rule for every AI crawler in the sources used here. Improve faults that the measurements demonstrate. Do not turn a fast test result into a claim about citations, or assume that an assistant’s absence proves the hosting is too slow.

Decide what happens next

Write a repair list with the evidence beside each item, then repeat the same technical checks after publication. Revisit the fixed buyer questions on an agreed schedule. Keep mentions, accurate descriptions, citations, visits and enquiries separate so a technical improvement cannot accidentally become a claimed sales result.

ScopeSite’s published H4TLT case study provides an approved example from workplace hearing surveillance. Its evidence belongs to that work and should be read directly, without borrowing its result for another sector.

V.O.I.C.E. remains the methodology and engine name. The earlier scanner keeps separate accounts and credits; purchased legacy credits do not expire or automatically become a subscription. Model API observations can differ from the consumer assistant applications.

Read the current scanner status or the recruitment discovery guide, then start with the question and page that matter to the next employer.

description: Web design in Frome costs between £500 and £30,000 depending on who you ask. Most of those quotes are either a waste of money or a rip-off.

When someone asks ChatGPT "who's the best [your trade] in Frome?", your £500 website is invisible.

blocks.after: Inspect the HTML returned by the server and compare it with the rendered page. If important content appears only after scripts run, some retrieval tools may miss it. title: How HTML structure and schema support a clearer website
description: How semantic HTML and accurate structured data support a clear website, and how to test them without claiming a guaranteed AI citation.

blocks.before: I've been digging into how AI systems actually read and recommend websites, and what I've found is this: the HTML structure of your page, the stuff that's been around since the 90s, is just as important as any fancy schema you bolt on top. And if you want ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google's AI to actually recommend your business? You need both working together, wrapped around content that's organised into proper information hubs. (We talk about getting found by ChatGPT in a separate article)
blocks.after: Clear headings, useful links and meaningful page structure help people use a page and make its content easier to inspect. Relevant structured data can describe the same supported facts. Neither format supplies a universal rule for whether ChatGPT, Perplexity or Google will recommend the business.

blocks.before: And here's something most guides won't tell you: you can use both. A 2024 study found that pages using semantic HTML structure alongside schema markup performed 43% better than pages using only one approach. The two reinforce each other.
blocks.after: Use semantic HTML and appropriate structured data where they serve the page. Test usability and validate the facts and markup, then measure any search or assistant outcome separately. The earlier 43% comparison is not supported by an identified primary study in this review.

blocks.before: At the schema level: You've got LocalBusiness schema with your address, opening hours, and service areas. Your solicitors have Person schema with their qualifications. Your FAQ page uses FAQPage schema so the AI can grab questions and answers directly.
blocks.after: At the schema level, describe the business, people and services only where the facts are supported and visible. FAQ markup should agree with the displayed questions and answers. Keep any subsequent citation claim tied to an observed provider response.

blocks.before: You don't need to choose between semantic HTML and schema markup. You need both. And you need them wrapped around content that's organised properly.
blocks.after: Use a clear page structure and relevant structured data together where they help the reader and describe the content accurately. Their presence does not guarantee a recommendation.

title: 3 SEO Mistakes Somerset Businesses Make (And How to Fix Them)
description: Practical checks for website speed, accurate structured data and ongoing search review, with separate evidence for assistant mentions and citations.

blocks.before: Here’s where it gets uncomfortable. Your website might look great. It might even load quickly. But if it doesn’t have proper schema markup, it’s invisible to the fastest-growing search channel in the world: AI.
blocks.after: Structured data can describe supported business facts and make eligible pages available for rich results. It must agree with the visible content. A valid graph cannot establish that an assistant understood, selected or recommended the business.

blocks.before: Schema markup is structured data written in JSON-LD format that tells search engines and AI systems exactly what your website is about. Not approximately. Not “probably a plumber in Taunton.” Explicitly: this is a plumbing business, based at this address, serving these areas, offering these services, run by this person with these qualifications.
blocks.after: Schema markup describes facts using a shared vocabulary. JSON-LD is one supported format, alongside Microdata and RDFa. The facts still need to be accurate and supported by the visible page.

blocks.before: 99.7% of websites don’t have this. That’s not a typo. Almost every website on the internet is effectively invisible to AI systems like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews because it lacks the structured data those systems need to make confident recommendations.
blocks.after: Check your own pages before drawing conclusions from a headline statistic. This review has no verified source for the earlier 99.7% claim. An absent schema block does not establish absence from an assistant’s answers.

blocks.before: The most important schema types for a Somerset business are LocalBusiness, Service, FAQPage, and BreadcrumbList. If you’re publishing blog content, add BlogPosting with SpeakableSpecification so AI knows which parts of your content are safe to cite and read aloud. If those terms mean nothing to you, that’s fine. But someone on your team, or your agency, needs to understand them. Because your competitors will.
blocks.after: Choose schema types that match the business and the content on each page. Describe genuine services, supported organisation facts and visible questions. SpeakableSpecification is not a general signal that a passage is safe for AI citation.

blocks.before: And here’s the thing that should genuinely worry you: pages with schema markup are 36% more likely to appear in AI-generated summaries and citations, according to WPRiders. A third more likely to be the answer. If you’re not in that 0.3% of websites with proper schema, you’re giving that advantage to someone else.
blocks.after: A citation claim needs evidence from the provider and questions being tested. The earlier percentages do not establish what will happen to your site. Keep validation results separate from actual mentions, citations and enquiries.

blocks.before: At ScopeSite, we built the V.O.I.C.E. methodology specifically to solve these three problems simultaneously. V.O.I.C.E. stands for Voice-Optimised, Organised, Intelligent, Content Engineering, Engineered. It’s a system that addresses speed, structured data, and ongoing visibility in one joined-up process.
blocks.after: V.O.I.C.E. is ScopeSite’s methodology and engine name. It covers website evidence, reviewed repairs and separate measurement of search performance and assistant answers.

blocks.before: Step 2: Check your schema. Go to Google’s Rich Results Test (search.google.com/test/rich-results) and enter your URL. If the result comes back empty or shows only basic WebSite schema, you’re missing the structured data that AI needs to understand and recommend your business. You should be seeing LocalBusiness, Service, and FAQPage at minimum.
blocks.after: Step 2: Inspect your structured data. Use Google’s Rich Results Test for its supported rich-result types and a general schema validator for wider markup. Confirm that the visible page supports every material claim. An empty rich-result test is not proof that no schema exists.

blocks.before: The fix isn’t a faster hosting plan. It’s a faster architecture. Server-side rendered websites built with modern tools like Next.js deliver fully-formed HTML to the browser in a single request. No waiting for JavaScript to load. No plugin overhead. No guesswork. That’s why ScopeSite sites consistently hit 100/100 on Google’s Lighthouse performance test. It’s not magic. It’s engineering.
blocks.after: Inspect the performance report before choosing the repair. Hosting, images, scripts, page structure and rendering can each contribute to a slow experience. Server rendering can deliver important content in the initial HTML, but it does not guarantee a particular Lighthouse score. Record the tested URL, device conditions and date.

title: SEO for Frome Businesses: How to Get Found on Google and AI in 2026
description: A practical guide to local search and AI discovery checks for Frome businesses, including readable pages, accurate business facts and recorded answers.

blocks.before: Ignoring schema markup. 99.7% of websites lack the structured data that AI systems need to understand and recommend businesses. An online retailer that added Product schema with reviews, pricing, and availability saw their click-through rate increase by 35%, according to Dynamic Schema. For a Frome business, schema is what makes the difference between being recommended by ChatGPT and being invisible to it. It’s not an advanced tactic anymore. It’s the baseline.
blocks.after: Check whether your structured data is accurate and useful for the page. There is no verified source here for the earlier 99.7% figure, and missing schema does not prove that ChatGPT cannot recommend the business. Any claimed improvement needs its own dated measurement.

blocks.before: Schema markup that actually tells AI something useful. Your website needs JSON-LD structured data that explicitly tells search engines and AI: this is a business called [name], located in Frome, Somerset, offering [services], with [reviews] and [credentials]. The important schema types for a Frome business are LocalBusiness, Service, FAQPage, and BreadcrumbList. If you’re blogging (and you should be), add BlogPosting with SpeakableSpecification so AI knows which content it can cite and read aloud.
blocks.after: Publish clear, supported business facts in the page and describe relevant facts in structured data. Choose types that fit the content. SpeakableSpecification identifies text for supported speech uses; it is not permission for every assistant to cite the passage.

blocks.before: Every blog post published on a ScopeSite-built website automatically generates six validated schema types: Articles, Breadcrumbs, FAQ, Local Businesses, Organisation, and Review Snippets. No plugins. No manual work. Google’s Rich Results Test confirms them all valid with zero errors. That’s the V.O.I.C.E. methodology at work.
blocks.after: The schema generated for a page depends on its template and content. Check the actual output and its supporting facts. A validator result belongs to that tested page and date; it does not certify every post or make review snippets appropriate on every article.

blocks.before: V.O.I.C.E. stands for Voice-Optimisation, for Intelligent, Crawler, Engines. It’s the methodology ScopeSite uses on every site we build.
blocks.after: V.O.I.C.E. is ScopeSite’s methodology and engine name. The current product page explains its relationship to CAFMO and the earlier scanner.

blocks.before: The auto-generated schema is a genuine differentiator. When you publish a blog post on a ScopeSite website, the system automatically creates interconnected structured data that tells AI what the post is about, who wrote it, which entities it references, and which sections are safe to cite. No manual configuration. No plugins to maintain. Publish and the schema handles itself.
blocks.after: Templates can generate structured data from approved content, but the output still needs review. When the page changes, check the graph, its relationships and its agreement with the visible facts. Automatic generation does not certify a claim or decide which passages an assistant will cite.

blocks.before: Type “Who is the best [your service] in Frome?” or “Can you recommend a [your business type] near Frome?” If you’re not mentioned, AI doesn’t know you exist. That’s the gap V.O.I.C.E. fills.
blocks.after: Write down a small set of questions a prospective customer might ask, then record the product, date, location, answer and cited URLs. An absent mention in one answer does not show that the model has no knowledge of the business. Repeat the same questions before drawing conclusions.

blocks.before: For competitive terms, expect 3-6 months before you see meaningful movement. For longer-tail, location-specific keywords like “web designer Frome” or “accountant near Frome,” results come faster, sometimes within weeks. AI visibility through V.O.I.C.E. typically shows results within 60-90 days of implementation.
blocks.after: The time needed depends on the website, the proposed changes and the question being measured. Agree the work and measurement schedule first. There is no verified general 60–90-day timetable for a business to appear in assistant answers.
